statement: In this work, we presented algorithm fair-bias and proved that it is O((log log log n)2 )- competitive for general metrics, and 9-competitive for tree metrics. Perhaps the first question is whether our algorithm (or indeed any algorithm) is O(1) competitive for (known or unknown) i.i.d arrivals for general metrics. Indeed, we do not know of any instances where Algorithm fair-bias’s performance is worse than O(1) competitive. However, it is not clear how to extend our proofs to establish an O(1) competitive ratio.
context: 5 Open Questions In this work, we presented algorithm fair-bias and proved that it is O((log log log n)2 )- competitive for general metrics, and 9-competitive for tree metrics. Perhaps the first question is whether our algorithm (or indeed any algorithm) is O(1) competitive for (known or unknown) i.i.d arrivals for general metrics. Indeed, we do not know of any instances where Algorithm fair-bias’s performance is worse than O(1) competitive. However, it is not clear how to extend our proofs to establish an O(1) competitive ratio. Another question is the relationship between the known and unknown i.i.d. models and the random order model. The optimal competitive ratios for the various arrival models for online problems can be sorted as follows (see e.g. [28, Theorem 2.1]) C.R.(Adversarial) ≥ C.R.(Random Order) ≥ C.R.(U nknown IID) ≥ C.R.(Known IID).
